newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Top Bosnian Croat nationalist buried with honours.
newsitem.headline: Top Bosnian Croat nationalist buried with honours.

text.p: Former Bosnian Croat nationalist leader Mate Boban, accused of pursuing the "ethnic cleansing" of Moslems in wartime, was celebrated as hero at a funeral ceremony on Wednesday in the Croat-held sector of Mostar.
Boban, 57, died two days ago of heart failure after suffering a brain haemorrhage.
Croat militia officers, political leaders and Roman Catholic Franciscans from Bosnia's Croat-held western Herzegovina region attended the service.
The mayor of Croat-controlled western Mostar, Mijo Brajkovic, declared a day of mourning in the multi-cultural town which Boban worked to divide while in a leadership position in 1992-94.
Boban was the president of the self-styled "Herceg-Bosna" mini-state which opposed multi-ethnic Bosnian statehood and sought union with neighbouring Croatia.
Human rights activists and Bosnian Moslem leaders said Boban was a war-crimes suspect linked to expulsions of Moslems and a brutal siege of Moslems in eastern Mostar.
Boban was never indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal in The Hague. His militia commander, General Tihomir Blaskic, is currently on trial for his role during the Moslem-Croat war.
Gojko Susak, defence minister from neighbouring Croatia, spoke at the funeral, saying Boban had led his community in difficult times.
Praising Boban for creating "the framework of statehood", he said: "We shall not betray what he began".
As war engulfed Bosnia, Boban met Bosnian Serb wartime leader Radovan Karadzic in Graz, Austria in May 1992 to draw up plans to divide the country's mixed population into "ethnically pure" areas.
Boban's army fought Serb forces early in the conflict but later waged war against its nominal Moslem allies in 1993 and early 1994.
The United States negotiated an end to the conflict and brokered the formation of a Moslem-Croat federation which has since been crippled by protracted nationalist quarrels.
In engineering the federation, Washington demanded the dismantling of the Herceg-Bosna administration and the removal of Boban, a loyal protege of Croatian President Franjo Tudjman.
Boban stepped down under U.S. pressure in February 1994. He was appointed an executive at the Croatian INA oil company based in Zagreb.
A cartoon in the Sarajevo daily newspaper Dnevni Avaz on Wednesday reflected the deep hostility felt by Bosnian Moslems towards Boban.
"You see, what The Hague can't do the devil can," said the cartoon.
